claims.text: CoCrFeNi is a medium-entropy alloy suitable for use as a transition material in HEA multilayers.
A thin CoCrFeNi interfacial layer can moderate the crossover between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep.
The CoCrFeNi layer can tailor interface coherency and local strain fields.
Tailoring coherency and local strain fields can balance the activation energies for vacancy diffusion and dislocation nucleation.
The initial HEA multilayer has largely coherent interfaces between its HEA layers.
The proposed transition layer is nanometer-scale and is placed at interfaces between the primary HEA layers.
Diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep may compete under the proposed high-temperature and applied-stress conditions.
The CoCrFeNi layer induces local interfacial strain and modifies interface coherency.
Modified interface coherency and strain alter vacancy-diffusion paths.
Modified interface coherency and strain alter the ease of dislocation nucleation at the interface.
CoCrFeNi has lattice parameters and bonding characteristics intermediate between those of the adjoining HEA layers.
The intermediate properties of the CoCrFeNi layer partially relieve local lattice-misfit strain.
Misfit-strain modulation lowers the barrier for dislocation activation at higher temperatures.
The CoCrFeNi transition layer retains some resistance to rapid diffusional flow at lower temperatures.
Adding the transition layer will produce a measurable shift from diffusion-mediated creep at lower temperature or stress to dislocation-mediated creep at higher temperature or stress.
HEA multilayers containing the CoCrFeNi transition layer will have better overall creep resistance than otherwise comparable multilayers without it.
Baseline HEA multilayers have relatively uniform and often high interface coherency that may favor one creep mechanism over the other.
The transition-layer effect will be significant only where diffusion and dislocation creep contributions are both non-negligible.
The influence of the transition layer may diminish at extremely high temperatures dominated by diffusion or at low temperatures where diffusion is negligible.
